text: Check the actual ceiling and how close you are to it: `cat /sys/fs/cgroup/pids.current` and `cat /sys/fs/cgroup/pids.max`. If current is sitting right up near max, that's not a general 'too many processes' feeling -- it's this container's hard pids-cgroup limit, and you're nearly out of runway for forking anything new at all (including your own commands).

Find what's still adding to the pool: `cat /var/run/pool-supervisor.pid` gives you its PID; `ps -p $(cat /var/run/pool-supervisor.pid) -o pid,cmd` (or just check `/var/log/pool-supervisor.log`) confirms it's still trying to add workers every time there's any headroom at all.

Stopping it is necessary but not sufficient: `sudo kill -9 $(cat /var/run/pool-supervisor.pid)` stops the *growth*, but every `job-worker` it already spawned is still alive and still holding a pid slot -- `pids.current` won't drop just because the supervisor is gone. Don't try to find them by process name/`comm` to kill them -- a worker that hit `exec sleep infinity` shows up in `ps`/`comm` as plain `sleep`, and a name-based `pkill` risks matching the wrong thing.

The supervisor kept its own record of exactly what it spawned: `cat /var/run/worker-pool/pids`. Kill every PID in that list precisely (`for p in $(cat /var/run/worker-pool/pids); do sudo kill -9 "$p"; done`), then re-check `/sys/fs/cgroup/pids.current` -- it should drop back down to just a handful, well clear of the ceiling.
